title: Type conversion and casting
learningGoals: predict what happens when types mix

youtube.title: C++ Type Conversion and static_cast | C++ Programming EP 09
youtube.description: In this episode you will predict what happens when types mix, convert with static_cast and avoid the integer-division trap, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Type conversion and casting · 1:24 Automatic conversion · 2:26 Conversion rules · 3:15 Second program · 4:39 Recap · 5:09 Bug of the Day · 6:09 Challenge · 6:32 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we mix types. Sometimes C plus plus changes a type for you. You must know when, and what is lost.

scenes.onScreen: "Type conversion and casting": numbered lines (1. C++ converts types for you; 2. A double becomes an int by cutting the decimals; 3. static_cast makes your choice clear) and an analogy card: pouring water from a jug into a small glass: some may be lost
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: C plus plus converts types when you mix them. An int becomes a double with no loss. A double becomes an int by cutting off the decimals. It does not round. A cast is a clear request to convert. In modern C plus plus, we write static cast. Think of a jug and a small glass. Pour the jug into the glass, and some water is lost. There are two kinds of conversion. The compiler does the first kind by itself, and we call it implicit. You ask for the second kind with a cast, and we call it explicit. Explicit is better, because the reader can see your intent. A cast says, yes, I know data may change here.
points: A double becomes an int by cutting the decimals

scenes.onScreen: convert.cpp: an int becomes a double, and a double becomes an int
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] Fish is an int with the value seven. [HL 6] We store it in a double. No loss happens. The weight is seven. [HL 7] Price is nine point nine nine. [HL 8] We store it in an int. The compiler cuts the decimals. [TRACK whole=9] Whole is nine, not ten. [HL 9] The first print shows seven. [HL 10] The second print shows nine. [HL 6] Seven becomes seven point zero. This conversion is safe, because every int fits inside a double. [HL 8] This conversion is not safe. The decimals are cut off, not rounded. Nine point nine nine becomes nine, and the program stays quiet about it. [HL 9] The first print shows the double with no decimals, because it ends in zero.

scenes.onScreen: a table: from type, to type and what happens
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: Look at the rules. Int to double is safe. Double to int cuts the decimals, so you lose data. Char to int gives the code of the letter. Bool to int gives one for true and zero for false. Notice the direction of each arrow. A small box into a big box is safe. A big box into a small box can lose data. Think of the jug and the glass again. Water poured from a glass into a jug is never lost.

diagram.caption: a table: from type, to type and what happens
rows: True is one, false is zero

scenes.onScreen: cast.cpp: static_cast converts a value on purpose
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 5] We have seven passed students out of eight. [HL 6] We cast passed to a double first. Then the division keeps the decimals. The answer is zero point eight seven five. [HL 8] Here we cast the letter A to an int. [HL 9] It prints sixty-five. That is the code of the letter A. [HL 6] Read the cast first. It turns a copy of passed into a double. The original variable does not change. After that, the double divided by an int gives a double. [HL 9] The letter A is stored as the number sixty-five. Every letter has its own code number.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as cast dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints zero point eight seven five, and then sixty-five. The ratio is zero point eight seven five, because seven out of eight is a little less than one.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. C plus plus converts types for you. Two. A double becomes an int by cutting the decimals. Three. Use static cast to convert on purpose. Four. Cast one number before you divide. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: C plus plus converts types for you.
A double becomes an int by cutting the decimals.
Use static cast to convert on purpose.
Cast one number before you divide.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Casting too late
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the program runs and the wrong output appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We cast the result of the division. The program prints zero. Why? Seven divided by eight is zero in int maths. The cast comes too late. Put the cast on one number, before the division. Then the answer is zero point eight seven five. Think of the order of work. First the division happens, and then the cast. If the division uses two ints, the damage is done before the cast starts. So cast one of the numbers first. Then the division already works with doubles.

scenes.onScreen: I tried to cast a spell on my double. It lost its decimals and its magic.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: I tried to cast a spell on my double. It lost its decimals and its magic.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: find the average of three marks
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Store three int marks. Print their average as a double with decimals. Hint: add the three marks as ints, and cast the sum to a double before you divide. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.onScreen: Next: EP 10 · auto, const and constexpr
scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: auto, const and constexpr. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Program output (it runs, but the answer is wrong):

0
bug.why: Seven divided by eight is already zero when both are ints. The cast then turns the zero into a double, which is too late.

pun: "I tried to cast a spell on my double. It lost its decimals and its magic."
challenge: Store three int marks. Print their average as a double with decimals. Hint: add the three marks as ints, and cast the sum to a double before you divide.
challengeAnswer: Add the three marks, cast the sum to a double, and divide by three. Use static cast before the division.
